title: Summary Ranges
description: A single left-to-right pass detecting and formatting maximal consecutive runs in a sorted, unique array.

blocks.text: Problem Summary: Given a sorted array of unique integers nums, return the smallest sorted list of ranges that exactly covers all the numbers in the array. Each range [a,b] should be represented as "a->b" if a is not equal to b, or just "a" if a equals b.

{"headers":["Signal in the problem","Pattern it points to"],"rows":[["\"Sorted array\" plus \"group consecutive runs\"","A single left-to-right pass, extending the current range while consecutive"],["Each range is maximal (cannot be extended further)","Close a range only when the next element breaks consecutiveness"]]}

blocks.text: Since nums is sorted and each value is unique, a "run" of consecutive integers is simply a maximal stretch where each element is exactly one more than the previous. Identifying these runs and formatting each as either a single value or a range covers the array exactly.

blocks.title: Analogy: Summarizing Attendance by Consecutive Days Present
blocks.text: Picture a list of the specific days someone attended an event, and wanting a compact summary like "Day 1 to 3, Day 5, Day 7 to 8" instead of listing every single day. Grouping consecutive days together, and listing lone days by themselves, gives the shortest accurate summary.

blocks.caption: Extend the current range while the next number is exactly one more; otherwise close it and start fresh

blocks.text: Result: ["0->2", "4->5", "7"]. 0,1,2 form one range; 4,5 form another; 7 stands alone.

Before checking every possible sub-range for consecutiveness, notice that a single left-to-right scan naturally identifies each maximal consecutive run: extend the current range as long as the next value continues it, and close it the moment it does not.

blocks.title: Building the Intuition
blocks.text:
Observation 1: Since nums is sorted and unique, checking if the next element continues the current run is just a single comparison: nums[j+1] equals nums[j] + 1.

Observation 2: Extending a pointer j forward while this holds correctly finds the END of the current maximal run in one pass.

Observation 3: Once the run ends (or the array ends), format it as "start" if start equals end, or "start->end" otherwise, and move to start the next run from the following element.

Observation 4: A single index sweeping through nums, always finding and formatting the next maximal run, covers the entire array in O(n) time.
This leads to a single pass: for each starting position, extend forward while consecutive, format the resulting run, and continue from the next unprocessed position.

For every possible starting position, check how far the consecutive run extends by scanning forward, then move past it and repeat, effectively the same idea but framed as explicitly re-deriving each run's boundary from scratch.

items: Start at the first unprocessed index.
Scan forward from there, checking one comparison at a time, until consecutiveness breaks.
Format the found range and repeat from the next unprocessed index.

codes.python:
def summary_ranges_brute(nums):
    n = len(nums)
    result = []
    i = 0
    while i < n:
        j = i
        while j + 1 < n and nums[j + 1] == nums[j] + 1:   # scan forward for the run's end
            j += 1
        result.append(str(nums[i]) if i == j else f'{nums[i]}->{nums[j]}')
        i = j + 1
    return result

blocks.text: Why the code is written this way

items: This directly and correctly identifies each maximal consecutive run using a nested scan.
This is already essentially the optimal single-pass approach; there is no meaningfully slower "brute force" alternative for this particular problem, since the direct approach is already O(n).

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(n), since the inner scan across all runs together only ever advances forward through the array once.
Space: O(1) extra beyond the output.

Note: for this particular problem, the natural direct approach is already the optimal O(n) solution; there is no separate slower brute force to meaningfully improve upon, since checking consecutiveness fundamentally requires examining each element once.

blocks.title: The Optimization Journey
blocks.text:
Since the natural approach is already O(n), "optimizing" here means writing the single-pass logic as cleanly and directly as possible, tracking just a start-of-run index and extending it forward.

Maintain a start index, and an inner pointer that extends forward while nums[pointer+1] equals nums[pointer]+1; once it stops, format the run using the start and current pointer positions.

Moving to the next run means resuming immediately after the just-closed run's end, ensuring the whole array is covered in one continuous pass.

The core idea: a single index sweep, tracking run starts and using a direct comparison to detect run continuation.
Maintain a start index for the current run. Extend forward while consecutive. Format the run once it ends, and continue from the next index, until the whole array is processed.

blocks.caption: A single pass extends the current run while consecutive, closing and formatting it otherwise

codes.python:
def summary_ranges(nums):
    result = []
    i = 0
    n = len(nums)
    while i < n:
        start = i
        while i + 1 < n and nums[i + 1] == nums[i] + 1:    # extend while consecutive
            i += 1
        result.append(str(nums[start]) if start == i else f'{nums[start]}->{nums[i]}')
        i += 1
    return result

blocks.text: Because nums is sorted and unique, a run of consecutive integers is exactly a maximal stretch where each successive value increases by exactly 1. The single pointer sweep correctly identifies the exact boundaries of every such run in one pass, since once consecutiveness breaks, that position can never be part of the current run, and the very next unprocessed index always begins a genuinely new run.
